chapters.title: Chapter 6: When to Hedge and When Not To

lessons.title: The Hidden Cost of Always Being Hedged

children.text: Chapter 5 priced a single hedge: roughly 4% of the portfolio a year for near-the-money protection, rolled quarterly. That is a number most investors nod at and then ignore, because 4% sounds survivable. Compound it across fifteen years of a long-term portfolio and it stops sounding survivable. This lesson runs the arithmetic over a full investing decade and a half, through a crash and through a calm stretch, so you can see what permanent protection actually does to wealth. The result is not a simple "never hedge". It is sharper than that, and it depends almost entirely on which strike you buy.

body.text: Permanent near-the-money hedging converts equity into something closer to a bond, and charges you equity-sized fees for the privilege. Permanent far out-of-the-money cover is a different animal: cheap enough to survive the good years and useful enough to matter in the bad ones.

children.text: Start with ₹25 lakh and run it for fifteen years down three routes. The return path is invented, not historical, but it has the shape Indian investors recognise: a good start, a savage crash, a strong recovery, a mid-cycle correction, and a decent finish.

body.caption: The three routes, with simplified annual assumptions

cells: Roll a put about 4% below the market every quarter
Roll a put about 10% below the market every quarter

body.text: These are deliberately simplified assumptions. A quarterly rolled hedge does not cap a calendar year's loss at a single neat number, because the floor resets at each roll, and real premiums move with volatility. The figures are chosen to be realistic in spirit, not precise. The point is the direction and scale of the effect, not the last rupee.

body.title: ₹25 lakh over 15 years through a crash path (₹ lakh)

children.text: Look at year 3, the crash year. The unhedged portfolio drops from ₹32.5 lakh to ₹19.5 lakh. The near hedge holds it at ₹24.5 lakh and the far hedge at ₹22.1 lakh. For several years afterwards, the hedged routes are ahead. Then the compounding of the premium starts to bite, and by year 15 the near hedge has fallen well behind. The far hedge, which cost a fifth as much, is still ahead.

body.caption: Where ₹25 lakh ends up after 15 years

body.text: The middle row is the lesson. Whether markets crashed or stayed calm, the permanently near-hedged investor ended up with roughly ₹59 lakh. Protection that thorough removes the bad outcomes and most of the good ones, so the result barely depends on what the market did. If that is what you want, you can buy it far more cheaply by simply holding less equity and more debt, with no premium, no rolling and no margin.

body.title: Read the table
body.question: Which statement is best supported by the two paths above?
options: Permanent near-the-money hedging produces a similar mediocre result whatever the market does
Far out-of-the-money cover beats holding unhedged in every market
A crash makes any hedge worthwhile
body.explanation: The near-hedged portfolio ended at roughly ₹59 lakh on both paths, because it gave up the upside as well as the downside. The far hedge helped in the crash path but still cost about ₹10.7 lakh in the calm path, so it does not win everywhere, and the first and last statements are both too sweeping.

children.text: Why Permanent Hedging Is So Expensive
Markets rise more often than they fall.
Insurance you buy every quarter on an asset that usually goes up will usually expire worthless. That is not a flaw. It is the design.
Every rupee of premium is a rupee that never compounds. Over fifteen years, 4% a year is not 60% of a portfolio, it is far more, because the lost money would itself have grown.
Sellers charge more than the expected payout.
Option sellers take real risk and want compensation for it, just as a general insurer does. On average, across many years, the buyer pays more than they collect.
Tax makes the payoff smaller than it looks.
As Chapter 5 showed, hedge gains are business income taxed at slab rates, so the rare win is trimmed while the frequent premium is paid in full.

body.title: What the premium would have become
body.prompt: An investor pays ₹1,00,000 of hedging premium in one year and never gets a payout. If that money had instead stayed invested and compounded at 11% a year for 15 years, what would it have grown to? Round to the nearest thousand rupees.
body.explanation: ₹1,00,000 × 1.11^15 = about ₹4,78,000. This is why a modest annual cost does so much damage over a long horizon: you lose the premium and everything it would have earned.

children.text: When Permanent Protection Is Still Defensible

body.title: Permanent hedging: when it makes sense and when it does not

columns.label: Defensible
points: Cheap far out-of-the-money cover, costing under about 1% a year
A retiree drawing an income, where a deep drawdown does permanent damage
A concentrated holding that cannot be sold, such as shares under lock-in
An investor with a proven history of panic selling, where the hedge buys discipline
Capital with a fixed end date, such as money earmarked for a purchase in two years

columns.label: Hard to defend
points: Near-the-money puts rolled continuously on a long-term portfolio
Hedging in the accumulation years, when falls help your SIPs
Hedging because markets feel high, which is a forecast, not a plan
Any hedge whose annual cost exceeds a fifth of your expected return
Protection you could get more cheaply by simply holding less equity

body.title: The cheaper substitute
body.textWithBlank: If you want permanently lower risk, the cheapest way to get it is usually to hold less ___, not to buy continuous protection.
body.explanation: Moving part of a portfolio to debt reduces both the downside and the upside, with no premium, no rolling and no margin. Options are better suited to temporary risks you expect to disappear.

body.title: The investor who wants to sleep at night
body.scenario: Ravi, 52, an orthopaedic surgeon in Jaipur, has ₹1.4 crore in equity funds and no near-term goal. He does not need the money for at least twelve years. After reading about the 2008 crash, he tells you he wants to hedge permanently with puts about 4% below the market, rolled every quarter, because he simply cannot stand the idea of losing half his money. He earns well and can afford the premium.
body.prompt: How would you respond to Ravi? Is he wrong to want permanent protection?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Take the fear seriously. Wanting to avoid a 50% drawdown is a legitimate preference, not a mistake, and telling him to simply be braver is useless advice.
2. But price what he is asking for. Near-money cover at about 4% a year on ₹1.4 crore is roughly ₹5.6 lakh a year, and over twelve years the compounded cost could easily exceed the crash he fears.
3. Show him the alternative that delivers the same feeling more cheaply: an asset allocation with, say, 65% equity and 35% debt. It cuts a 50% market crash to about a 33% portfolio fall, costs nothing in premium, and needs no rolling or margin.
4. If he still wants options, steer him to far out-of-the-money cover at well under 1% a year. It does nothing in ordinary corrections but limits a catastrophe, which is the risk he actually described.
5. Ask the diagnostic question: in March 2020, would he have sold? If yes, the hedge may be worth paying for as a behavioural tool, and that is a real benefit even though it never appears in a return calculation.
The lesson: match the solution to the fear. Ravi fears catastrophe, not volatility, and catastrophe cover is the cheap part of the options market.

body.title: Does it matter when the crash arrives?

children.text: Yes, and in a way that favours hedging less than people expect. In the path above, the crash lands in year 3, when the portfolio is still small in rupee terms. The hedge saves about ₹5 lakh at that point, then pays premium on a growing portfolio for twelve more years.

Move the same crash to year 13 and the arithmetic changes completely: the hedge protects a much larger portfolio, and there are fewer remaining years of premium to drag on it. This is the same sequence risk you met in Chapter 1, seen from the hedger's side. It is also the reason hedging becomes more attractive as a portfolio grows large relative to your future contributions, and as the date you need the money comes closer.

body.title: Stress-test your own hedging plan
steps: Write down your intended annual hedging cost as a percentage of the portfolio.
Multiply your current portfolio by that percentage to get this year's rupee cost, then project it over your investing horizon.
Compare that figure with the size of the loss you are trying to avoid, and be honest about how often you expect that loss.
Price the alternative: what mix of equity and debt would give you a similar worst case with no premium?
If you still want a hedge, check whether the cheapest far out-of-the-money strike covers the risk you actually fear.

body.label: The one-fifth rule of thumb
body.value: If annual hedging cost exceeds about a fifth of your expected return, think again
body.context: On an expected 11% return, that is roughly 2.2% a year. Near-money protection at 4% a year fails this test comfortably. Far out-of-the-money cover at 0.8% passes.

body.title: The Cost of Always Being Hedged

cards.definition: Keeping protection in place continuously, rolling it at every expiry, regardless of conditions.
The compounding effect of hedging costs on long-term wealth, which is far larger than the annual percentage suggests.
Far out-of-the-money protection that is cheap enough to hold permanently and only matters in a severe fall.
Holding less equity and more debt, which lowers risk permanently without paying premium.
The benefit of a hedge that keeps an investor from panic selling, which never shows up in a return calculation.

points: Over fifteen years, permanent near-the-money hedging produced roughly the same result whether markets crashed or stayed calm, because it removed the upside along with the downside.
In the calm path, that protection cost about ₹43.8 lakh on a ₹25 lakh starting portfolio.
Far out-of-the-money cover at under 1% a year was cheap enough to survive the good years and helpful enough to win in the crash path.
Premium compounds against you: ₹1 lakh of premium is nearly ₹4.8 lakh of lost wealth over fifteen years at 11%.
If you want permanently lower risk, holding less equity is almost always cheaper than buying continuous protection.
Permanent hedging is defensible for retirees, locked-in concentrated holdings, proven panic sellers and money with a fixed end date.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The return paths are invented illustrations, not forecasts or historical data, and the hedging assumptions are simplified. Different assumptions produce different results. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before setting a hedging policy.
